questions.detail: A precise answer is that inspection found boundary selection could move start backward and eventually repeat it. The existing bounds-only test missed termination. A bounded trace demonstrated the repeated state. The intended fix is strict forward progress and parameter validation with edge-case regressions. As of this guide, the source remains unchanged. If you later implement it, update the story with actual tests and outcomes rather than presenting the proposal as completed work.
questions.follow: What evidence separates an observed defect from a speculative risk?

questions.question: Which claims should you avoid in interviews about this project?
questions.quick: Do not claim embeddings, a vector database, an LLM, durable multi-tenancy, verified citations, or production deployment are already implemented.
questions.detail: Also avoid saying that 94.76% code coverage means 94.76% answer accuracy, that the regexes solve injection, that async means parallel CPU execution, that document hashing deduplicates uploads, or that Docker proves production readiness. The strength of the project is its inspectable baseline and your reasoning about improvement. Accurate scope makes deeper technical follow-ups easier to answer.
questions.follow: How would you correct yourself if you accidentally called the lexical vectors embeddings?

questions.question: How do you answer an unfamiliar RAG design question?
questions.quick: Clarify the required behavior, state assumptions, reason from data and failure boundaries, and propose a measurable experiment.
questions.detail: If you do not know an index parameter or model behavior, say so and explain how you would verify it in official documentation and a benchmark. Use fundamentals: where evidence comes from, who can access it, how it is selected, how the answer is supported, and what happens on failure. Avoid inventing a universal best chunk size or latency number. Tradeoff reasoning is more transferable than memorizing vendor names.
questions.follow: What information would you ask before estimating capacity or choosing a model?

questions.question: What should you be able to demonstrate before the interview?
questions.quick: Explain the code, run upload/query and abstention examples, calculate similarity and metrics, diagnose failures, and sketch a measured production design.
questions.detail: Practice a five-minute architecture walkthrough, a two-minute current-scope pitch, and coding drills for cosine, chunk progress, and idempotency. Be ready to point to routes, RagService, ports, adapters, settings, tests, and deployment files. Explain why the next steps are ordered as they are. Use the matching question IDs in the revision and detailed guides to revisit weak topics; no question bank can guarantee every possible interviewer prompt.
questions.follow: Can you explain the full pipeline aloud without using a framework name as the explanation?

title: Additional backend interview depth
overview: These topics often appear when an AI interview turns into a backend design discussion. They are not all implemented here, but understanding them helps explain how a mobile-facing RAG API becomes a reliable shared service.

questions.question: How do JWT and OAuth differ?
questions.quick: JWT is a claims/token representation; OAuth is an authorization framework, and a signed JWT is not necessarily encrypted.
questions.detail: A backend validating a JWT must verify signature, allowed algorithm, issuer, audience, expiration, and relevant claims under its identity design. Decoding the payload alone establishes no trust. OAuth describes delegated access flows and roles; its access tokens need not be JWTs. Our shared API key implements neither. For a mobile product, use a suitable identity system and current platform/security guidance rather than inventing an authentication protocol. References: [JWT](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519) and [OAuth framework](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749).
questions.follow: Why does a validly signed token for another API not authorize access to ours?

questions.question: What is a connection pool?
questions.quick: A connection pool reuses a bounded set of database or HTTP connections instead of creating one for each operation.
questions.detail: Connections cost setup time and server resources. Size pools with total replicas and worker processes in mind: ten workers each allowing twenty database connections can demand two hundred. Long-held connections or transactions can queue requests. Acquire for the needed scope, release reliably, set deadlines, and reset tenant/session state safely. Create process-owned pools during lifespan and close them at shutdown. Our memory adapter has no connection pool.
questions.follow: Why can simply increasing pool size overload the database?

questions.question: What do database indexes and transaction isolation add?
questions.quick: Indexes accelerate selected access patterns; isolation defines what concurrent transactions can observe and modify safely.
questions.detail: A B-tree index on tenant and document identity serves a different purpose from a vector ANN index. Indexes consume storage and write work, so choose them from actual queries. Isolation affects races such as concurrent updates or publishing conflicting active versions; constraints and version checks enforce important invariants. Do not assume all databases or default isolation levels provide the same behavior. Our current list has no database transaction semantics.
questions.follow: Which index would help a highly selective tenant filter before vector scoring?

questions.question: What are ORMs, migrations, and SQL injection?
questions.quick: An ORM maps code to database operations, migrations version schema changes, and parameterized queries help prevent SQL injection.
questions.detail: An ORM can simplify access but does not remove the need to understand queries, indexes, transactions, and authorization. Migrations should be reviewed and compatible with rollout/rollback requirements. Never concatenate user text into SQL commands; use bound parameters and least-privilege roles. A future text-to-SQL model adds another untrusted query source requiring validation and restricted execution. No ORM or migration system is currently installed as an application component.
questions.follow: Can an ORM query still accidentally omit a tenant filter?

questions.question: Are FastAPI BackgroundTasks a durable job queue?
questions.quick: No; post-response in-process tasks do not provide durable distributed job ownership or recovery by themselves.
questions.detail: They can be useful for limited work after sending a response, but a worker crash can lose unfinished work. Expensive parsing and embedding across many documents needs explicit persistence, job state, retries, and bounded workers. The current project does not use BackgroundTasks either. Use the right mechanism for the completion guarantee, not merely an API that makes the response return earlier. Reference: [FastAPI background tasks](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/background-tasks/).
questions.follow: What happens to an in-process task during container replacement?

questions.question: How should cancellation and structured concurrency work?
questions.quick: Tie related tasks to a request or job scope, propagate cancellation deliberately, and ensure cleanup without assuming completed side effects are undone.
questions.detail: If an Android user navigates away, cancelling the client request may stop some server work, but an already committed upload remains. For independent concurrent retrieval branches, manage child-task lifetimes and exceptions together. Release resources in cleanup paths and decide whether accepted ingestion jobs outlive the HTTP connection. CPU loops without suspension require a different execution strategy. Reference: [Python coroutines and tasks](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html).
questions.follow: Which work should continue after a client disconnects, and why?

questions.question: What should you know about Python CPU work, the GIL, and GPUs?
questions.quick: Async is for cooperative concurrency; CPU/GPU execution requires deliberate runtime and worker design, not an async keyword.
questions.detail: Traditional GIL-enabled CPython limits concurrent Python bytecode execution in one process, while native libraries can release the GIL and Python builds differ. Avoid universal claims about all Python versions. CPU-bound Python work often benefits from separate processes; model inference may use native/GPU execution and batching. GPU memory, model residency, batch size, and queueing determine serving capacity. Our current scorer is ordinary Python CPU work.
questions.follow: Why might a thread pool help blocking I/O more than pure Python token-count computation?

questions.question: How should pagination and payload limits be designed?
questions.quick: Bound list sizes and request/response sizes, and use stable pagination contracts for growing document collections.
questions.detail: Future document listing should not return the entire corpus. Cursor pagination can avoid some shifting-page problems under updates, but the ordering and snapshot semantics must be defined. Query result counts, citation excerpts, filenames, request IDs, and generated answer length also deserve bounds. Our API has upload/query limits and a top_k cap, but no document listing or full transport-body policy.
questions.follow: What happens to offset pagination when documents are inserted between requests?

questions.question: How should exceptions be translated across layers?
questions.quick: Adapters expose meaningful internal failures, services apply business policy, and routes translate outcomes into stable public errors.
questions.detail: Do not leak vendor stack traces, SQL strings, or secrets to clients. Distinguish invalid input, missing authorization, unavailable dependencies, timeouts, and internal bugs. Our route catches selected decoding and policy exceptions; everything else reaches a generic 500 response. A full model gateway needs richer internal categories and observable causes so the client can retry appropriately without learning confidential internals.
questions.follow: Should a provider rate-limit failure always be presented as the user exceeding their own quota?

questions.question: How do network partitions affect consistency and availability?
questions.quick: When systems cannot communicate, you must define which operations fail, wait, or serve possibly stale data while preserving required invariants.
questions.detail: Do not reduce distributed design to “pick any two” without specifying the partition and operation. A tenant permission revocation may require refusing stale cached access, whereas an explicitly stale public answer may be acceptable. Replication lag, index lag, and queue delay are different consistency problems. State the product’s guarantees, failure policy, and recovery process. Our single-process baseline has no distributed replication or partition-handling design.
questions.follow: Would you serve cached confidential evidence if current authorization cannot be verified?

title: Additional model and evaluation interview depth
overview: These questions connect RAG engineering to the model concepts an AI interviewer may probe. They supplement the system design; implementing a transformer or fine-tuning a model is not part of the current repository.

questions.question: What is attention in a transformer?
questions.quick: Attention computes context-dependent combinations of token representations so tokens can use information from other permitted positions.
questions.detail: The familiar scaled dot-product form uses query/key similarities to weight value vectors, with masking where required. These attention queries are model-internal vectors, not the same object as our user’s HTTP question or a database query. Transformer architectures differ, but this mechanism helps explain why a model can relate parts of a context and why context length has compute implications. Reference: [Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762).
questions.follow: How does causal masking differ from an encoder reading a whole passage?

questions.question: How are retrieval embeddings trained with contrastive learning?
questions.quick: Training rewards relevant query-passage pairs relative to negative passages so compatible encoders learn useful retrieval geometry.
questions.detail: A common objective increases the positive pair’s similarity compared with negatives in a batch or mined candidate set. Negative quality, labeling errors, and domain coverage affect what the model learns. The resulting space is task-specific, not a universal semantic truth map. This motivates held-out evaluation and careful handling of hard negatives. Our term-frequency vectors are manually computed counts and have no training objective.
questions.follow: Why can in-batch negatives accidentally include another relevant passage?

questions.question: How do TF-IDF, BM25, sparse learned retrieval, and dense retrieval differ?
questions.quick: They use lexical weights, saturated probabilistic-style lexical scoring, learned sparse term weights, and learned dense vectors respectively.
questions.detail: TF-IDF weights terms by local frequency and corpus rarity, while BM25 adds its own saturation and length normalization. Learned sparse models can expand or weight vocabulary terms with a neural model. Dense models represent text in a compact continuous space. Each has strengths for exact terms, paraphrases, storage, and scoring infrastructure. Our baseline uses raw TF cosine, so it is neither TF-IDF nor BM25 nor a learned sparse model.
questions.follow: Why should you identify the exact baseline instead of calling every lexical method BM25?

questions.question: What is SPLADE?
questions.quick: SPLADE learns sparse vocabulary-based representations with term expansion for first-stage retrieval.
questions.detail: It uses a neural model to assign sparse term weights, including useful terms beyond literal input matches. This can bridge lexical and semantic behavior while using sparse retrieval infrastructure. Learned expansion can still introduce noise and requires model/version and index management. It is an alternative retrieval component to evaluate, not something our Counter implements. Reference: [SPLADE paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.05720).
questions.follow: How is learned sparse expansion different from manually adding synonyms?

questions.question: What is Dense Passage Retrieval or DPR?
questions.quick: DPR uses compatible question and passage encoders to retrieve passages through dense-vector similarity.
questions.detail: The question and passage sides can be trained jointly with relevance supervision. Document representations can then be indexed, while a new question is encoded at query time. This illustrates why retrieval embeddings are trained for matching and why compatibility matters. DPR is a research architecture, not a vector database or a generator. Reference: [Dense Passage Retrieval paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906).
questions.follow: Where does DPR end and answer generation begin?

questions.question: What is ColBERT?
questions.quick: ColBERT uses contextual token representations and late interaction to score fine-grained query-passage matches efficiently.
questions.detail: Rather than collapsing a passage to a single vector, it retains token-level information and combines token matches at scoring time. This can improve discrimination while adding storage and retrieval-system complexity. Compare the actual variant and implementation against single-vector and reranking baselines under the same constraints. Reference: [ColBERT paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12832).
questions.follow: Why is ColBERT not simply a cross-encoder run on every document?

questions.question: What is LoRA and does it replace RAG?
questions.quick: LoRA trains low-rank parameter updates for adaptation; it does not replace retrieval of current authorized evidence.
questions.detail: LoRA is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning approach that can reduce trainable parameters compared with full adaptation. It changes model behavior through training, while RAG changes available context at inference. A system may use both if evaluation justifies it. Neither LoRA nor model fine-tuning exists in our repository. Reference: [LoRA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685).
questions.follow: Would you use LoRA to implement document deletion from a changing knowledge base?

questions.question: How do candidate recall, context precision, and answer quality connect?
questions.quick: Retrieval must find useful evidence, packing must retain the right parts, and generation must use them correctly; failure at any stage can dominate.
questions.detail: A high-recall candidate set can still become a poor prompt if duplicates or long irrelevant passages crowd out the answer. A perfect prompt can still yield an unsupported claim from the generator. Measure stages separately and run ablations such as oracle context or no-reranker comparisons. Do not optimize a single retrieval metric without checking supported-answer outcomes and resource cost.
questions.follow: Why can increasing candidate count improve recall but reduce final answer quality?

questions.question: What does calibrated confidence mean?
questions.quick: A calibrated confidence estimate matches observed correctness frequencies on a defined population; similarity scores are not automatically calibrated.
questions.detail: If responses assigned 0.8 confidence are correct about 80% of the time under a stable rubric and distribution, the estimate is calibrated in that sense. Build and validate such estimates on held-out data and monitor drift. Retrieval similarity, model token probability, and self-reported confidence measure different things and may correlate poorly with task correctness. Our grounded boolean and citation score should not be presented as calibrated confidence.
questions.follow: How would you test calibration separately from ranking quality?

questions.question: How do annotation quality and uncertainty affect evaluation?
questions.quick: Clear relevance rubrics, multiple reviewers where needed, disagreement review, and uncertainty reporting make metric conclusions more trustworthy.
questions.detail: Two passages may support different valid interpretations, and a source may be outdated or partially relevant. Define graded labels, query scope, source versions, and abstention criteria. Review disagreements instead of silently treating one label as unquestionable truth. Small test sets can make apparent improvements unstable, so include confidence intervals or paired error inspection. Good evaluation is a maintained data product, not just a script that prints a score.
questions.follow: How would you revise an ambiguous question without biasing the evaluation toward one system?
